tags.why: Raises rainy-day fund cap and changes how deposits interact with the spending limit, giving more flexibility.
Larger reserves support continued program spending in downturns.
Creates a large loan program to help middle-income buyers of new homes.
Uses revenue bonds repaid by borrowers, not general-fund debt.
Authorizes $8.4B general-obligation bonds for immunology research.
Directs substantial public capital to a specific research institute and grants.

quality.detail: Half the bond proceeds are directed to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute, raising questions about competitive allocation and long-term oversight.

tags.why: Imposes a one-time 5% tax on net worth of billionaires.
Raises tens of billions for health care and related programs outside normal spending rules.
Exempts the new revenue from the constitutional spending limit and school-funding guarantee.

quality.detail: Requires the state to value a wide range of hard-to-price assets (private business interests, art, IP, etc.) on a short timeline; likely litigation and valuation disputes.
Props 41 and 42 were written in part to constrain or nullify effects of a wealth tax of this type.

tags.why: Forces new special-tax revenues into the spending limit and requires audits.
Makes it harder to enact taxes that bypass existing fiscal constraints.
Prohibits new state personal-property (wealth-like) taxes and certain retroactive taxes.
Limits future revenue tools that could expand spending.
Raises the vote threshold for voter-proposed local special taxes from majority to two-thirds.
Makes it harder for local governments to raise new revenue.
Adds state oversight and penalties on nonprofit community clinics’ spending.

quality.detail: “Program services” advancing charitable purpose is broadly defined; opponents argue it could penalize legitimate administrative, research, or facility costs and disrupt care.

tags.why: Sets hard deadlines, narrows alternatives analysis, and limits lawsuit remedies for most housing and infrastructure projects.
Designed to accelerate housing and related infrastructure by reducing process delays (moves toward removing barriers / speeding overall supply).

quality.detail: Applies to a very broad set of “essential” projects; environmental groups argue it reduces public comment windows and court oversight more than necessary.

changes.reason: Exempting revenue from the spending limit increases flexibility (side B). Previous sign was inverted relative to the A/B definitions.
Forcing new revenue into the spending limit strengthens restraint (side A). Previous sign was inverted.
Limiting future revenue tools that expand spending strengthens restraint (side A). Previous sign was inverted.
Raising the threshold to two-thirds is exactly side A of the definition. Previous sign was inverted.
Speeding approvals by reducing process delays moves toward side A (remove barriers / increase overall supply). Previous sign treated it as the subsidized-unit focus (side B).
Giving more flexibility on the rainy-day / spending-limit interaction is side B. Previous sign was inverted.
Revenue bonds repaid by borrowers do not add general-fund debt service (side A). Previous sign treated it as accepting GO bonds (side B).
